```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4.5)
```

```{r}
library(pgmcompR)
```

Undirected models describe symmetric interactions. A Markov network (Markov
random field) defines
$$P(x) = \frac{1}{Z} \prod_{c} \phi_c(x_c), \qquad Z = \sum_x \prod_c \phi_c(x_c),$$
with nonnegative potentials $\phi_c$ that need not be probabilities.

## A small Ising model

Three binary spins on a triangle, each pair preferring agreement:

```{r}
st <- list(A = c("-", "+"), B = c("-", "+"), C = c("-", "+"))
agree <- function(a, b, w = 2) discrete_factor(c(a, b), st[c(a, b)], c(exp(w), 1, 1, exp(w)))
field <- discrete_factor("A", st["A"], c(1, 3))
mn <- markov_network(list(agree("A", "B"), agree("B", "C"), agree("C", "A"), field))
mn
partition_function(mn)
query(mn, "C")
query(mn, "C", evidence = list(B = "-"))
```

The external field on `A` pulls the other spins toward `+` through the
couplings. Exact queries use the same variable elimination and junction tree
engines as Bayesian networks.

```{r}
query(mn, c("A", "C"), method = "jt")
```

## Separation

In an undirected graph, $X$ and $Y$ are independent given $Z$ whenever every
path from $X$ to $Y$ passes through $Z$:

```{r}
chain <- markov_network(list(agree("A", "B"), agree("B", "C")))
separated(chain$graph, "A", "C", "B")
f_ac <- query(chain, c("A", "C"), list(B = "+"))
f_a <- query(chain, "A", list(B = "+"))
f_c <- query(chain, "C", list(B = "+"))
all.equal(factor_values(f_ac), as.numeric(outer(factor_values(f_a), factor_values(f_c))))
```

## Factor graphs

A factor graph is a bipartite graph between variables and factors. It makes
the factorization explicit: two models with the same Markov network can have
different factor graphs (one triangle potential versus three pairwise ones).

```{r}
fg <- factor_graph(list(agree("A", "B"), agree("B", "C"), agree("C", "A")))
fg
```

```{r, eval = requireNamespace("igraph", quietly = TRUE)}
plot(fg)
```

## Converting between model families

A Bayesian network converts to a factor graph (one factor per CPD) or a
Markov network (its moral graph); the distribution is unchanged and
$Z = 1$.

```{r}
asia <- example_network("asia")
asia_fg <- as_factor_graph(asia)
partition_function(asia_fg)
all.equal(query(asia_fg, "lung", list(xray = "yes")), query(asia, "lung", list(xray = "yes")))
nrow(edges(as_markov_network(asia)$graph))
```

Independencies that need the directions, such as `asia` and `smoke` being
marginally independent, are lost in the moral graph:

```{r}
d_separated(asia, "asia", "smoke")
separated(moralize(asia), "asia", "smoke")
```

## Belief propagation

Sum product belief propagation computes all single variable marginals at
once. It is exact on tree shaped factor graphs:

```{r}
bp <- belief_propagation(chain)
bp
```

On the triangle it is loopy and approximate:

```{r}
lbp <- loopy_bp(mn)
lbp$beliefs$C
query(mn, "C")
```

Max product propagation gives max marginals and the most probable joint
state on trees:

```{r}
belief_propagation(chain, type = "max")$assignment
mpe_query(chain)$assignment
```

## Sampling

Gibbs sampling works on any discrete model with a positive distribution:

```{r}
query(mn, "C", method = "gibbs", n = 4000, seed = 1)
```
